description: Key claims of the five thinkers (plus Hardy-Weinberg and the Price equation, added 2026-11-01 as the one-formalization control and the identity case for the `formalization` tag) that GPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude, asked without a candidate list, most often named as having testable claims closest to theorem status. Every DOI below was checked against Crossref on 2026-10-30 (title and year match). Years are Crossref's issued years.

claims.label: Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection (partial-change form)
claims.statement: The rate of increase in mean fitness of a population due to natural selection equals its additive genetic variance in fitness at that time.
claims.notation: \Delta_{NS}\bar{w} = V_A(w)/\bar{w} (discrete generations); \left.\frac{d\bar{m}}{dt}\right|_{NS} = V_A(m) for Malthusian fitness m
claims.context: Assumptions: the 'partial change' holds average effects of alleles and the environment fixed (Price 1972, Ewens 1989); V_A is the additive genetic variance in fitness. Formal status: proved in this partial-change reading. Read as a claim about the total change in mean fitness it is false under dominance, epistasis, frequency dependence or a changing environment.
claims.proposed_test: In a pedigreed wild population or an experimental-evolution line, estimate the additive genetic variance in relative fitness (animal model) and compare it with the observed per-generation response of breeding values for fitness, separating the selection term from environmental deterioration.

paper.title: The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection

readings.name: partial-change
readings.statement: The partial rate of change in mean fitness attributable to natural selection, holding average effects and environment fixed, equals V_A(w)/w̄ (Price 1972, Ewens 1989).

readings.name: total-change
readings.statement: The total rate of change in mean fitness equals V_A(w)/w̄.
readings.status: false under dominance, epistasis, frequency dependence or environmental change

formalization.note: Okasha (BJPS 59, 2008) distinguishes the two readings; the proof attaches to the first only, and only the second is what a population measurement tests.

claims.label: Fisher-KPP wave of advance of an advantageous gene
claims.statement: An advantageous allele spreading through a continuous population advances as a travelling wave whose speed is set by the selection coefficient and the diffusion (dispersal) rate.
claims.notation: u_t = D u_{xx} + s u(1-u); travelling waves u(x-ct) exist iff c \ge c^* = 2\sqrt{sD}; compactly supported initial data spread at asymptotic speed c^*
claims.context: Assumptions: one spatial dimension (extended to R^n), constant diffusion D, logistic (genic) selection with coefficient s, deterministic large-population limit. Formal status: proved; Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov (1937) gave the proof independently, and Aronson and Weinberger (1978) proved the asymptotic spreading speed in several dimensions. Finite populations, Allee effects or long-tailed dispersal change the speed.
claims.proposed_test: Measure the front speed of a beneficial allele, or of an expanding population, in an experimental range expansion (e.g. bacteria on agar or laboratory insect arenas) with independently measured s and D, and compare it with 2*sqrt(sD).

paper.title: The wave of advance of advantageous genes

formalization.note: Minimal front speed 2\sqrt{rD} for the scalar reaction-diffusion equation with compactly supported initial data.

claims.label: Fisher's principle of equal investment in the sexes
claims.statement: Under random mating and autosomal inheritance, selection drives parents to invest equally in sons and daughters, which gives a 1:1 sex ratio when the two cost the same.
claims.notation: ESS allocation: N_m c_m = N_f c_f; with c_m = c_f the unbeatable primary sex ratio is 1:1
claims.context: Assumptions: panmixia, autosomal control of the sex ratio, each offspring has one father and one mother, no local mate competition or sex-specific resource competition. Formal status: proved as an invasion (ESS) result (Shaw and Mohler 1953). Its own named exceptions (local mate competition, Hamilton 1967) are predicted deviations, not refutations.
claims.proposed_test: Compare population sex-investment ratios (numbers times per-offspring cost) across species that meet the panmixia assumption, and test that experimentally perturbed sex ratios return toward equal investment.

paper.title: The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection

formalization.note: Equal parental investment is the ESS under panmixia; LMC exceptions are predicted deviations, not alternative formalizations.

claims.label: Fisher's infinitesimal model of quantitative inheritance
claims.statement: Continuous traits determined by many Mendelian loci of small additive effect produce the observed correlations between relatives, so biometric and Mendelian inheritance are consistent.
claims.notation: Cov(z_i, z_j) = 2\Theta_{ij} V_A + \Delta_{ij} V_D; in the limit of M \to \infty loci the offspring trait given parents is Gaussian with mean (z_1+z_2)/2 and segregation variance V_0(1-\bar{F}), with error O(1/\sqrt{M}) (Barton, Etheridge and Veber 2017)
claims.context: Assumptions: many unlinked loci of small additive effect, random mating, environmental effects independent of genotype. Formal status: the covariance decomposition is proved; the infinitesimal limit, including under selection, is proved by Barton, Etheridge and Veber (2017). Large-effect loci and epistasis break the Gaussian limit.
claims.proposed_test: Compare observed correlations between relatives of different degree in large pedigrees with 2*Theta*V_A + Delta*V_D, and check that the within-family segregation variance stays near V_0(1-F) under selection, as the limit theorem predicts.

paper.title: The Correlation between Relatives on the Supposition of Mendelian Inheritance

formalization.note: The infinitesimal limit of Barton, Etheridge and Véber (2017) is the single modern formalization.

claims.label: Turing diffusion-driven instability
claims.statement: A homogeneous steady state of two reacting chemicals that is stable without diffusion can become unstable to spatial perturbations when the chemicals diffuse at different rates, spontaneously producing a pattern.
claims.notation:
u_t = f(u,v) + D_u 
abla^2 u, v_t = g(u,v) + D_v 
abla^2 v; with tr J < 0 and det J > 0, instability at some wavenumber k iff D_v f_u + D_u g_v > 2\sqrt{D_u D_v \det J}, which requires D_u 
e D_v
claims.context: Assumptions: two species, smooth kinetics, linearization about a homogeneous steady state, fixed domain without growth or mechanics. Formal status: the linear instability conditions are proved; existence and stability of nonlinear patterns are proved for many specific models but not in general.
claims.proposed_test: Measure the reaction Jacobian and the diffusivities of a candidate morphogen pair independently, check that the inequality holds, and then confirm that perturbing the diffusivity ratio switches patterning on or off.

paper.title: The chemical basis of morphogenesis

formalization.note: Linear instability conditions of the homogeneous steady state; nonlinear pattern existence is a separate, model-specific question, not a second reading of this claim.

claims.label: Turing wavelength selection
claims.statement: The spacing of a Turing pattern at onset is set by the reaction rates and diffusivities, not by the size of the tissue, so changing these parameters predictably changes the number of repeated elements.
claims.notation: at onset k_c^2 = \sqrt{\det J/(D_u D_v)}, \lambda_c = 2\pi/k_c; under uniform rescaling of D, \lambda \propto \sqrt{D}
claims.context: Assumptions: near onset of instability, two species, domain large compared with the wavelength. Formal status: proved by linear analysis. Away from onset, the selected wavelength depends on nonlinear terms and history.
claims.proposed_test: Alter morphogen production, degradation or diffusion in a developing tissue (e.g. Hox dosage or Bmp/Wnt inhibition in mouse limb buds) and test whether digit or element number changes in the direction and proportion the dispersion relation predicts.

paper.title: The chemical basis of morphogenesis

formalization.note: Wavelength at onset from the fastest-growing linear mode.

claims.label: Reaction-diffusion of morphogens accounts for biological pattern
claims.statement: Chemical substances that react and diffuse through tissue (morphogens) are sufficient to account for the main phenomena of morphogenesis.
claims.notation: no canonical formalization: the claim asserts that a biological pattern is generated by a system of the form u_t = F(u) + D\nabla^2 u with D not proportional to the identity
claims.context: Formal status: a framework rather than a mathematical proposition. Kondo and Asai (1995) confirmed the predicted stripe-branching dynamics in Pomacanthus and Castets et al. (1990) produced Turing patterns chemically. Mechanical buckling, prepatterns and cell-cell signalling can produce the same patterns, so a matching pattern alone does not identify the mechanism.
claims.proposed_test: In a candidate system, identify the interacting molecules, measure their kinetics and diffusion, and confirm novel predictions such as stripe insertion during growth or pattern change after a targeted perturbation, while ruling out mechanical alternatives.

paper.title: The chemical basis of morphogenesis

formalization.note: A research framework, not a proposition with a formalization.

claims.label: Kimura fixation probability of a mutant allele
claims.statement: The probability that a mutant allele eventually fixes in a finite population depends on its initial frequency, its selective advantage and the effective population size, and equals its initial frequency when it is neutral.
claims.notation: u(p) = \frac{1-e^{-4N_e s p}}{1-e^{-4N_e s}}; neutral limit u(p) = p, so a new mutant fixes with probability 1/(2N)
claims.context: Assumptions: diffusion approximation to the Wright-Fisher model, genic (additive) selection with coefficient s, constant effective size N_e, no linkage to other selected sites. Formal status: proved within the diffusion limit.
claims.proposed_test: Track the fate of many marked mutations of measured fitness effect in replicate experimental populations of known N_e (e.g. barcoded microbial lineages) and compare fixation frequencies with u(p).

paper.title: On the probability of fixation of mutant genes in a population

formalization.note: Diffusion-limit fixation probability (1 - e^{-2s})/(1 - e^{-4Ns}).

claims.label: Neutral substitution rate equals the mutation rate
claims.statement: For neutral mutations the long-run rate of molecular substitution equals the mutation rate per generation, independent of population size, which yields a molecular clock.
claims.notation: k = 2N\mu \cdot \frac{1}{2N} = \mu
claims.context: Assumptions: strictly neutral mutations, mutation rate constant per generation, steady state. Formal status: an exact consequence of the neutral fixation probability. Variation in generation time and weak selection on nearly neutral sites cause departures from strict clock-like rates.
claims.proposed_test: Compare the substitution rate at putatively neutral sites (synonymous sites, pseudogenes) across lineages with independently measured per-generation mutation rates from pedigree sequencing.

paper.title: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level

formalization.note: Substitution rate k = 2N\mu \cdot 1/(2N) = \mu is an algebraic consequence of neutral fixation probability (identity); that observed rates equal the mutation rate is the contingent claim.

claims.label: Mean time to fixation of a neutral mutant
claims.statement: A neutral mutant that does go to fixation takes on average about four times the effective population size, in generations, to do so.
claims.notation: \bar{t}_1(p) = -\frac{4N_e(1-p)\ln(1-p)}{p}; as p = 1/(2N) \to 0, \bar{t}_1 \to 4N_e generations
claims.context: Assumptions: diffusion approximation to the Wright-Fisher model, neutrality, constant N_e. Formal status: proved within the diffusion limit (Kimura and Ohta 1969).
claims.proposed_test: In replicate small populations of known N_e, record the conditional time to fixation of neutral marker alleles and compare it with 4N_e generations.

paper.title: The average number of generations until fixation of a mutant gene in a finite population

formalization.note: Mean conditional fixation time 4N generations in the diffusion limit.

claims.label: Neutral equilibrium heterozygosity (Kimura-Crow)
claims.statement: Under neutral mutation to new alleles and drift, expected heterozygosity reaches an equilibrium that rises with the product of effective population size and mutation rate.
claims.notation: H = \frac{\theta}{1+\theta}, \theta = 4N_e\mu (infinite-alleles model)
claims.context: Assumptions: infinite-alleles mutation, neutrality, constant N_e, equilibrium. Formal status: proved within the model. Observed diversity varies far less across species than census sizes predict (Lewontin's paradox; Leffler et al. 2012), which points to linked selection and demography.
claims.proposed_test: Regress genome-wide neutral diversity on independent estimates of N_e times mu across species, and test whether the residual pattern is explained by linked selection.

paper.title: The number of alleles that can be maintained in a finite population

formalization.note: Equilibrium heterozygosity 4N\mu/(1+4N\mu) under infinite alleles; Lewontin's paradox is the data side.

claims.label: Neutral theory: most molecular substitutions are neutral
claims.statement: Most evolutionary changes at the molecular level are caused by random drift of selectively neutral or nearly neutral mutations, not by positive selection.
claims.notation: empirical claim: for most sites |N_e s| \lesssim 1, so the fraction of substitutions driven by positive selection \alpha is small; tested with d_N/d_S and McDonald-Kreitman \alpha = 1 - \frac{D_s P_n}{D_n P_s}
claims.context: Formal status: not a mathematical statement; an empirical claim about the distribution of fitness effects. King and Jukes (1969) proposed it independently. Genomic estimates of alpha and pervasive linked selection are cited against its strong form (Kern and Hahn 2018).
claims.proposed_test: Estimate the proportion of adaptive substitutions (alpha) with McDonald-Kreitman-type tests genome-wide across many species, correcting for slightly deleterious polymorphism and demography.

paper.title: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level

formalization.note: An empirical claim about the distribution of fitness effects.

claims.label: Hamilton's rule
claims.statement: A gene for social behaviour increases in frequency when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by genetic relatedness, exceeds the cost to the actor.
claims.notation: \Delta \bar{p} > 0 \iff r b - c > 0, with r, b, c defined as regression coefficients (Queller form via the Price equation)
claims.context: Assumptions: in Hamilton's original derivation, additive fitness effects and weak selection; in the general form, b and c are partial regressions of fitness on the actor's and the partner's genotype. Formal status: proved; exact in the regression form (Gardner, West and Wild 2011). Critics argue that the general form is close to an identity with little predictive content (Nowak, Tarnita and Wilson 2010).
claims.proposed_test: In a cooperative system (social insects, cooperatively breeding birds, microbes), estimate r from genotypes and b and c from fitness measurements, and test whether rb > c predicts which individuals help.

paper.title: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. I

readings.name: regression form
readings.statement: rb > c with r, b, c the partial regression coefficients of the Price-equation decomposition (Gardner, West and Wild 2011).

readings.name: causal/phenotypic form
readings.statement: An altruistic trait spreads when genealogical relatedness times fitness benefit exceeds fitness cost, with b and c as fixed payoffs.
readings.status: holds only under additivity and weak selection

formalization.note: The regression form is exact because its coefficients are defined to make it so; the phenotypic form is the one tested in the field.

claims.label: Haplodiploidy hypothesis for eusociality
claims.statement: Because full sisters in haplodiploid species share three quarters of their genes, more than a mother shares with her offspring, haplodiploid insects are predisposed to evolve sterile worker castes.
claims.notation: with a singly mated queen, r_{sister,sister} = 3/4 > r_{mother,daughter} = 1/2, but r_{sister,brother} = 1/4
claims.context: Formal status: the relatedness coefficients are proved. The explanatory claim is largely abandoned: the low sister-brother relatedness offsets the gain unless the sex ratio is biased, diploid termites are eusocial, and comparative work points to ancestral monogamy instead (Hughes et al. 2008).
claims.proposed_test: Use phylogenetic comparative analysis to test whether eusociality arises more often in haplodiploid than in diploid lineages after controlling for ancestral mating system.

paper.title: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. II

formalization.note: Relatedness coefficients 3/4 (sister-sister) and 1/4 (sister-brother) are proved; the explanatory claim is contingent and largely abandoned.

claims.label: Local mate competition sex ratio
claims.statement: When a few mothers lay eggs on a patch and their offspring mate there before the daughters disperse, the evolutionarily stable sex ratio is female-biased, and the bias weakens as the number of mothers grows.
claims.notation: unbeatable proportion of males x^* = \frac{n-1}{2n} for n foundresses per patch (diploid case)
claims.context: Assumptions: n foundresses per patch, mating confined to the natal patch, only females disperse, mothers control the sex ratio. Formal status: proved as an ESS within the model. Haplodiploidy and inbreeding shift x* slightly.
claims.proposed_test: Vary the number of foundresses per host in a parasitoid wasp (e.g. Nasonia) and compare the offspring sex ratio with (n-1)/(2n).

paper.title: Extraordinary Sex Ratios

formalization.note: Unbeatable sex ratio (n-1)/2n under local mate competition.

claims.label: Declining force of selection with age
claims.statement: The strength of selection on survival falls with age after reproduction begins, so senescence is an inevitable outcome of natural selection.
claims.notation: s(a) = \frac{\partial r}{\partial \ln p_a} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{x=a+1}^{\infty} e^{-rx} l_x m_x, non-increasing in a
claims.context: Assumptions: an age-structured population with fixed age-specific fertility and no growth or repair after maturity. Formal status: the formula for s(a) is proved. The inevitability claim is refuted as stated: Jones et al. (2013) found species with flat or declining mortality with age, consistent with life histories where fertility rises with size.
claims.proposed_test: Compare age trajectories of mortality and fertility across many species with the trajectories that s(a) predicts from each species' own life table.

paper.title: The moulding of senescence by natural selection

readings.name: sensitivity formula
readings.statement: The force of selection on age-specific survival, s(a) = \sum_{x>a} l_x m_x e^{-rx} / T, is non-increasing in a.

readings.name: inevitability
readings.statement: Mortality must therefore rise with age in every species.

formalization.note: The formula is a theorem about the model; the inevitability claim added assumptions the model does not supply.

claims.label: Evolutionarily stable strategy conditions
claims.statement: A strategy is evolutionarily stable if, once common, it cannot be invaded by any rare alternative strategy.
claims.notation: I is an ESS iff for all J \ne I: E(I,I) > E(J,I), or E(I,I) = E(J,I) and E(I,J) > E(J,J); every ESS is an asymptotically stable rest point of the replicator dynamics (Taylor and Jonker 1978), not conversely
claims.context: Assumptions: an infinite, well-mixed population with pairwise interactions and asexual or clonal inheritance of strategies. Formal status: the definition is exact, and the link to replicator dynamics is proved. Finite populations, mutation and genetic constraints can stop an ESS from being reached.
claims.proposed_test: In a system with measurable payoffs (microbial public-goods strains, contest behaviour), estimate the payoff matrix and test that the predicted ESS composition resists experimental invasion by rare alternative strategies.

paper.title: The Logic of Animal Conflict

formalization.note: Definition plus the asymptotic-stability link to replicator dynamics.

claims.label: Hawk-Dove mixed ESS
claims.statement: When the cost of injury exceeds the value of the contested resource, the stable outcome is a mixture in which animals escalate with probability equal to the ratio of resource value to injury cost.
claims.notation: payoffs E(H,H) = (V-C)/2, E(H,D) = V, E(D,H) = 0, E(D,D) = V/2; for C > V the unique ESS plays Hawk with probability p^* = V/C
claims.context: Assumptions: symmetric pairwise contests, fixed V and C, no role asymmetries (asymmetries such as ownership give the Bourgeois ESS instead). Formal status: proved within the game.
claims.proposed_test: Experimentally vary resource value and the expected cost of fighting in a contest system, and test that escalation frequency tracks V/C.

paper.title: Evolution and the Theory of Games

formalization.note: Mixed ESS p* = V/C when V < C.

claims.label: War of attrition ESS
claims.statement: In contests settled by display, where the animal willing to persist longer wins and costs grow with time, the stable strategy is to choose a persistence time at random from an exponential distribution whose mean equals the resource value.
claims.notation: with cost linear in time at unit rate and resource value V, the ESS persistence time has density p(x) = \frac{1}{V} e^{-x/V}
claims.context: Assumptions: symmetric contests, cost linear in display time, no information about the opponent's choice. Formal status: proved (Maynard Smith 1974); existence and uniqueness in the generalized game proved by Bishop and Cannings (1978).
claims.proposed_test: Record contest durations in a display-based contest system and test for an exponential distribution, with the mean scaling with experimentally varied resource value.

paper.title: The theory of games and the evolution of animal conflicts

formalization.note: Exponential persistence-time distribution as the unique ESS (Bishop and Cannings 1978).

claims.label: Twofold cost of sex
claims.statement: An asexual mutant female in a sexual population with equal sex ratio produces twice as many grandchildren as a sexual female, so sex needs a compensating advantage of up to twofold to persist.
claims.notation: with equal fecundity and a 1:1 sex ratio, the odds of asexual to sexual females double each generation: \frac{q_{t+1}}{1-q_{t+1}} = 2\frac{q_t}{1-q_t}
claims.context: Assumptions: anisogamy with males contributing no resources, equal fecundity and viability of sexual and asexual females, a 1:1 sex ratio. Formal status: proved as a population-dynamic identity under these assumptions. Its biological force depends on how often those assumptions hold.
claims.proposed_test: In a species with coexisting sexual and asexual lineages, measure relative per-capita growth of asexual versus sexual females in a common environment and compare it with the predicted factor of 2.

paper.title: The Evolution of Sex

formalization.note: Under equal fecundity and a 1:1 sex ratio the twofold rate difference is bookkeeping (identity); whether those assumptions hold in a population is the contingent part.

claims.label: Genetic hitchhiking (selective sweep)
claims.statement: When a favourable mutation sweeps to fixation, it reduces genetic variation at closely linked neutral sites, and the reduction is larger the tighter the linkage relative to the strength of selection.
claims.notation: the relative heterozygosity H_{after}/H_{before} at a neutral site at recombination fraction c is an increasing function of c/s that tends to 0 as c/s \to 0; the affected region has a width of order s in recombination units, up to logarithmic factors in N
claims.context: Assumptions: a single sweep from a new mutation, deterministic allele-frequency trajectory, two loci. Formal status: proved under these approximations (later refined in coalescent treatments). Background selection produces a similar correlation between diversity and recombination.
claims.proposed_test: Test for a positive correlation between neutral diversity and local recombination rate across the genome, and for diversity troughs around sites of recent adaptive substitution, while modelling background selection as the alternative.

paper.title: The hitch-hiking effect of a favourable gene

formalization.note: Reduction in linked neutral diversity after a sweep, under the deterministic-sweep approximation.

claims.thinker: G. H. Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg
claims.label: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
claims.statement: In an infinitely large, randomly mating diploid population with no selection, mutation or migration, the genotype frequencies at a biallelic autosomal locus reach p^2, 2pq, q^2 after a single generation and stay there, with allele frequencies unchanged.
claims.notation: f(AA) = p^2,\; f(Aa) = 2pq,\; f(aa) = q^2,\quad p + q = 1
claims.context: Assumptions: infinite population, random mating, non-overlapping generations, no selection, mutation, migration or drift, autosomal biallelic locus. Formal status: proved (Hardy 1908; Weinberg 1908, independently). The equilibrium is reached in one generation for an autosomal locus and asymptotically for X-linked loci.
claims.proposed_test: In a large population sample of genotype calls (e.g. 1000 Genomes), compare genotype counts at biallelic SNPs with the p^2, 2pq, q^2 expectation; deviations localize to selection, population structure, inbreeding or genotyping error.

paper.title: Mendelian Proportions in a Mixed Population

formalization.note: Hardy-Weinberg is the control case: a single formalization everyone agrees on, with a direct genotype-count test.

claims.label: The Price equation (covariance form)
claims.statement: For any population partitioned into entities i with fitness w_i and character value z_i, the change in the population mean character between generations equals the covariance of fitness with character plus the fitness-weighted mean of within-entity transmission change, each divided by mean fitness.
claims.notation: \bar{w}\,\Delta\bar{z} = \mathrm{Cov}(w_i, z_i) + \mathrm{E}(w_i\,\Delta z_i)
claims.context: Assumptions: a well-defined parent-offspring mapping and finite means; no genetic or dynamical assumptions at all. Formal status: proved; it is an algebraic identity that holds for any partition of any population (Price 1970, 1972). Its content as a statement about selection depends on how the two terms are interpreted.
claims.proposed_test: Not directly testable as an identity. Testable uses: partition a measured change in a trait into the selection and transmission terms in a pedigreed population and check that the terms are stable across alternative partitions.

paper.title: Selection and Covariance

formalization.note: The covariance decomposition holds for any partition of any population (identity). Where the line between the selection term and the transmission/environment term is drawn is a modelling choice the equation does not force; that choice is the contingent part (doctor_memory, Moltbook, 2026-11-01).
